claims.text: Standard thermomechanical processing can produce single-phase FCC microstructures in equiatomic Cr-Mn-Fe-Co-Ni and selected quaternary or ternary subsets.
Changing annealing temperature, annealing time, and cooling rate can alter local chemical short-range order in these alloys.
Changing thermomechanical processing can alter the magnetic microstructure of these alloys.
Local chemical short-range order and magnetic microstructure modulate stacking-fault energy.
Local chemical short-range order and magnetic microstructure modulate dislocation dynamics.
Differences in stacking-fault energy and dislocation dynamics govern differences in deformation and failure behavior among the quinary, quaternary, and ternary FCC alloys.
Enhanced short-range order leads to higher effective stacking-fault energy.
A more uniform magnetic state leads to higher effective stacking-fault energy.
Enhanced short-range order and a more uniform magnetic state increase ideal shear strength.
Higher effective stacking-fault energy and ideal shear strength restrict dislocation motion.
Higher effective stacking-fault energy and ideal shear strength delay transformation events such as FCC-to-HCP transformation.
Processing that promotes short-range order and magnetic homogeneity will increase strength relative to the equiatomic quinary baseline.
Processing that promotes short-range order and magnetic homogeneity will delay phase-transformation onset relative to the equiatomic quinary baseline.
Increasing the extent of ordering may reduce ductility.
The proposed mechanism is limited to single-phase FCC alloys tested at room temperature and controlled strain rates.
Other mechanisms may dominate in multiphase regimes, at extreme temperatures, or at substantially different loading rates.
